messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (mean at 0.7-0.8s).
        *   $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (absolute maximum).
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (ripple at 0.7-0.8s).
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (cold start to 1.8V).
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{V}$ (stability between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s).
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $\approx 3.2\text{V}$ (at S1).
    *   Operating Conditions:
        *   S1: Nominal.
        *   S2: Heavy load ($R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$).
        *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($I_p = 100\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 2.2\text{M}\Omega$).
        *   S4: Weak excitation ($I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 1\text{M}\Omega$).
        *   S5: Low frequency ($f = 80\text{Hz}$).
        *   S6: High $C_p$, high temp.

    *   FBR (Full-Bridge Rectifier) fails:
        *   S2 (Heavy load): $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ (Inefficient energy extraction).
        *   S3 (Strong excitation): $V_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$ (No overvoltage protection).
        *   S4 (Weak excitation): $V_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ (Too much drop/inefficient).
        *   S5 (Low freq): $dV$ fail (Unstable/slow convergence).
    *   The FBR has a high forward voltage drop and doesn't match the impedance of the piezo.

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* This is the gold standard for piezo energy harvesting. It uses a switch and inductor to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively flipping the charge and significantly increasing extracted power.
    *   *Standard Bridge + Zener:* Needed to prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding $3.6\text{V}$.
    *   *Buck/Boost:* Too complex/high power cost for this level of excitation unless simplified.
    *   *Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI):*- This usually looks like a bridge with an inversion circuit on the piezo side.

    *   **Topology 1: Synchronous Inversion (SSHI-like) + Rectifier.**
        To implement a simple SSHI:
        - Piezo is connected to a rectifier.
        - A switch and inductor are used to flip the voltage of $C_p$ at the peaks of the current.
        - Actually, a simpler version is a "Parallel-SSHI" or a "Synchronous Switch".
        - Let's try: Piezo terminals (pzp, pzn). A rectifier to the output. An inductor-switch path to flip $C_p$.
        - Wait, the components allowed are a bit limited. We have `S` (switches) and `SYNC`.
        - A standard SSHI involves a switch that shorts $C_p$ through an inductor $L$ at the voltage extrema.
        - Circuit:
            - Full bridge (DSCH) from (pzp, pzn) to (out, 0).
            - Switch S1 and Inductor L1 in series across (pzp, pzn) to flip the voltage.
            - This would increase the voltage amplitude across the bridge.
            - Add a Zener (DZ33) to clamp $V_{out}$ to 3.3V.
            - Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ to filter ripple.

    *   **Topology 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge).**
        - Using switches instead of diodes to reduce the voltage drop.
        - However, the SYNC controller is limited (max 2). A full synchronous bridge requires 4 switches.
        - We can use a "Half-bridge" or a combination.
        - Let's try a "Synchronous Charge Pump" or a simpler SSHI variation.

    *   **Topology 3: SSHI with a different configuration.**
        - Instead of a full bridge, use a half-wave rectifier if the excitation is strong enough, but full-wave is generally better.
        - Or use a "Buck-converter" style approach if we can. But the SYNC controller is tied to the piezo peaks.

    *   *Design 1 (SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener):*
        - Rectifier: D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn).
        - SSHI Flip: S1(pzp, n1), L1(n1, pzn).
        - Sync G1: `edges: both`, `ton` $\approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
        - Protection: DZ33(0, out).
        - Storage: C_out(out, 0).

    *   *Design 2 (Active Rectification / Sync-Switching):*
        - Use SYNC to switch the piezo directly into the capacitor.
        - S1(pzp, out) and S2(pzn, out) controlled by G1 and G2.
        - G1 (edges: pos), G2 (edges: neg).
        - This replaces the diodes for the top part of the bridge.
        - Keep D3, D4 for the bottom part to ground.
        - Add DZ33(0, out).
        - Storage: C_out(out, 0).

    *   *Design 3 (Simple Bridge + Zener - Baseline Improvement):*
        - Just a Full Bridge and a Zener. (Actually, FBR failed on $V_{avg}$ in S2 and S4, so just adding a Zener won't help the low-voltage cases).

    *   *Wait, let's refine the SSHI.*
        The most effective simple SSHI circuit for these constraints is often a bridge rectifier combined with an inductive flipping circuit.
        The flipping happens at the peaks of the voltage. The SYNC controller "closes its switches... at the piezo voltage extrema". This is perfect for SSHI.
        $L$ value: $\pi\sqrt{L C_p} = ton$. If $ton$ is $10-100\mu\text{s}$ and $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, then $L \approx (ton/\pi)^2 / C_p$.
        For $ton=50\mu\text{s}$, $L \approx (1.6 \times 10^{-5})^2 / 25\text{nF} \approx 10\text{mH}$. (Max L is 10mH).

    *   *Checking the a-priori screening:*
        SSHI increases the voltage seen by the rectifier, which helps S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation).
        The Zener DZ33 prevents $V_{out}$ from exceeding 3.6V in S3.
        A large $C_{out}$ (e.g., 10-47uF) helps with ripple and $dV$.

    *   *Refining Design 1 (SSHI + Bridge):*
        - Components:
            - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
            - D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
            - D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
            - D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
            - L1: pzp -> n1
            - S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
            - G1: SYNC (edges: both, ton: 50us, phase: 0)
            - DZ1: 0 -> out (DZ33)
            - C1: out -> 0 (value: 22uF)

    *   *Refining Design 2 (Active Switch Rectification):*
        - Instead of a bridge, use SYNC to transfer charge.
        - S1: pzp -> out (ctrl: G1)
        - S2: pzn -> out (ctrl: G2)
        - G1: SYNC (edges: pos, ton: 1ms, phase: 0)
        - G2: SYNC (edges: neg, ton: 1ms, phase: 0)
        - This is more like a synchronous rectifier.
        - Need to ensure the current only flows *into* the capacitor.
        - If S1 is closed and $V_{pzp} < V_{out}$, charge flows back.
        - So, synchronous rectification usually needs the switch to open when $V_{pzp}$ drops below $V_{out}$.
        - The SYNC controller closes for `ton` at the extrema. This isn't a full synchronous rectifier. It's more of a pulsed charge transfer.
        - Let's stick to SSHI as the primary strategy.

    *   *Refining Design 3 (P-SSHI):*
        - In a Parallel SSHI, the inductor is used to flip the voltage across the piezo capacitor before it is rectified.
        - Let's try a version with a capacitor $C_{flying}$ and switches (a charge pump), but we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
        - Let's try a "Half-Bridge" SSHI.
        - D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
        - G1: SYNC (edges: both)
        - C1: out -> 0
        - DZ1: 0 -> out (DZ33)
        - Wait, the FBR results showed $V_{avg}$ was too low for S2/S4. An SSHI is the best way to boost that.

    *   L1: 10mH
    *   Cout: 22uF (Try to keep ripple low and $dV$ low)
    *   ton: $\pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \times 25\text{nF}} \approx \pi \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx \pi \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.5\text{ms}$.
    *   Wait, `ton` limit is $1\text{ms}$.
    *   If $ton = 1\text{ms}$, $L = (1\text{ms}/\pi)^2 / 25\text{nF} \approx (3.18 \times 10^{-4})^2 / 25\text{nF} \approx 10 \times 10^{-8} / 25\text{nF} \approx 4\text{mH}$.
    *   Let's use $L=4.7\text{mH}$ and $ton=1\text{ms}$.

    *   *Bridge components:* 4 diodes.
    *   *SSHI components:* 1 L, 1 S, 1 SYNC.
    *   *Protection/Storage:* 1 DZ33, 1 C.
    *   Total: 8 components. (Limit 16).

    *   S3 (Strong excitation): $V_{out}$ can go high. DZ33 limits it to $\approx 3.3\text{V} + \text{leakage}$. This should keep $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   S2/S4 (Low power): SSHI flips the voltage, increasing the effective $V_{peak}$ across the bridge, which improves $V_{avg}$.
    *   S5 (Low freq): The SYNC controller tracks frequency, so it should be stable.
    *   $t_{up}$: Cold start might be slow, but SSHI is more efficient than FBR.

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener** (Classic SSHI)
    *   **Proposal 2: SSHI + Half Bridge + Zener** (To see if lower diode drop helps)
    *   **Proposal 3: Active Synchronous Transfer** (Using SYNC to pump charge)

    *Let's refine Proposal 2:*
    - Half-bridge: D1(pzp, out), L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn), G1(SYNC), DZ1(0, out), C1(out, 0).
    - This only harvests the positive half-cycle. Probably worse than FBR.

    *Let's refine Proposal 3 (Synchronous Transfer):*
    - S1(pzp, out), S2(pzn, out).
    - G1(SYNC, edges: pos, ton: 1ms), G2(SYNC, edges: neg, ton: 1ms).
    - This is a synchronous rectifier.
    - Since it's only "on" for 1ms at the peak, it acts like a sampled-data converter.
    - This might be very efficient.
    - Let's add a Zener DZ33(0, out) and C1(out, 0).

    *Wait, for Proposal 3 (S1, S2), if $V_{out}$ is 3V and $V_{pzp}$ is 3.2V, the switch S1 connects them. If $V_{pzp}$ drops to 2.9V, the switch is still closed for the remainder of `ton`, so charge flows back. But `ton` is very short (1ms) compared to the period (10ms). So the backflow is minimal.*

    Let's try:
    - Proposal 1: SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener.
    - Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectifier (S1, S2) + Zener.
    - Proposal 3: SSHI + Synchronous Rectifier. (S1, S2 as rectifiers, L1/S3 as flipper).

    *Actually, let's keep it simple for the first round.*
    Proposal 1: Full Bridge + SSHI flip + Zener clamp.
    Proposal 2: Full Bridge + Zener clamp + larger C (just to see, but maybe too similar to FBR). No, let's do something different.
    Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectifier (S1, S2) + Zener clamp.
    Proposal 3: a "Voltage Doubler" / Charge Pump using SYNC.

    *Let's re-evaluate Proposal 1 (SSHI Full Bridge):*
    - D1: pzp, out
    - D2: pzn, out
    - D3: 0, pzp
    - D4: 0, pzn
    - L1: pzp, n1
    - S1: n1, pzn (ctrl: G1)
    - G1: SYNC, edges: both, ton: 1ms
    - DZ1: 0, out (DZ33)
    - C1: out, 0

    *Let's re-evaluate Proposal 2 (Synchronous Rectifier):*
    - S1: pzp, out (ctrl: G1)
    - S2: pzn, out (ctrl: G2)
    - G1: SYNC, edges: pos, ton: 1ms
    - G2: SYNC, edges: neg, ton: 1ms
    - DZ1: 0, out (DZ33)
    - C1: out, 0
    - (Wait, this needs a way to prevent the piezo from discharging the capacitor when the switch is closed but $V_{piezo} < V_{out}$. Diodes in series with switches could help, but that's just a bridge. Let's use the switches to *bypass* the diodes).
    - S1: pzp, n1; D1: n1, out. (S1 acts as a switch). No, that's not right.
    - Let's try: S1: pzp, out (ctrl: G1), G1: SYNC (edges: pos, ton: 1ms). This is the simplest synchronous transfer.

    *Let's re-evaluate Proposal 3 (Modified Bridge - "Self-Synchronized" like):*
    - D1: pzp, out
    - D2: pzn, out
    - S1: pzp, 0 (ctrl: G1)
    - S2: pzn, 0 (ctrl: G2)
    - G1: SYNC (edges: pos)
    - G2: SYNC (edges: neg)
    - (This is not a standard topology).

    *Let's stick to the most promising:*
    1.  SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener (Best for power boost).
    2.  Active Rectification (S1, S2) + Zener (Best for low drop).
    3.  Full Bridge + Zener + high $C_{out}$ (Baseline with protection).

    *Self-Correction on Proposal 2:*
    Synchronous Rectification with `S` and `SYNC`:
    S1: pzp, out (ctrl: G1), G1: edges: pos, ton: 1ms.
    S2: pzn, out (ctrl: G2), G2: edges: neg, ton: 1ms.
    This will transfer charge at the peaks. It's effectively a switched-capacitor converter.

    *Final check on components for Proposal 1:*
    - D1: ["pzp", "out"], DSCH
    - D2: ["pzn", "out"], DSCH
    - D3: ["0", "pzp"], DSCH
    - D4: ["0", "pzn"], DSCH
    - L1: ["pzp", "n1"], 4.7mH
    - S1: ["n1", "pzn"], ctrl: G1
    - G1: SYNC, ton: 1ms, edges: "both", phase: 0
    - DZ1: ["0", "out"], DZ33
    - C1: ["out", "0"], 22uF

    *Final check on components for Proposal 2:*
    - S1: ["pzp", "out"], ctrl: G1
    - S2: ["pzn", "out"], ctrl: G2
    - G1: SYNC, ton: 1ms, edges: "pos", phase: 0
    - G2: SYNC, ton: 1ms, edges: "neg", phase: 0
    - DZ1: ["0", "out"], DZ33
    - C1: ["out", "0"], 22uF

    *Final check on components for Proposal 3:*
    - D1: ["pzp", "out"], DSCH
    - D2: ["pzn", "out"], DSCH
    - D3: ["0", "pzp"], DSCH
    - D4: ["0", "pzn"], DSCH
    - DZ1: ["0", "out"], DZ33
    - C1: ["out", "0"], 47uF (Just a protected FBR).

    *Wait, Proposal 3 is just a protected FBR. Let's try to make it more interesting.*
    How about a "Half-Wave SSHI" (only flipping one side)? No, Full-Bridge SSHI is better.
    What if we use a larger inductor and shorter $ton$ for SSHI? The evolution strategy will optimize $L$ and $ton$ anyway.

    *One detail:* $V_{max}$ in S3 was 5.72V for FBR. DZ33 (Zener) should definitely be there to keep it under 3.6V.

    *Wait, the SYNC controller closes at the "piezo voltage extrema".*
    For SSHI, you want to flip the voltage *at* the extrema.
    The current $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ is zero at the voltage extrema.
    The SYNC controller closes at the zero crossings of the piezo current. This is exactly when the voltage is at its peak. Perfect.

    *Let's double check the Zener:*
    "DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)".
    To clamp `out` to 3.3V, the cathode must be at `out` and anode at `0`.
    `["0", "out"]`. Correct.
